content: 1. In populations where the prevalence of anemia among non-pregnant women of reproductive age is 20% or higher, improving hemoglobin concentration and iron status is essential to reduce the risk of anemia. 2. For obese adolescents, family-based, multi-component lifestyle weight management services should be developed and supported. These services should include nutrition, physical activity, and psychosocial support, and they should be delivered by multi-professional teams as part of Universal Health Coverage (UHC). 3. A pilot cash transfer program in northern Ecuador, implemented from July to December 2019, aimed to improve the diet of pregnant adolescent girls. This program was a collaboration between three government ministries, the World Food Programme (WFP), and Plan International. 4. The program targeted communities at high risk of gender-based violence and teenage pregnancy, particularly in rural and peri-urban areas where poverty was prevalent. Participants received cash transfers equivalent to USD $50 to cover the costs of recommended diets they could not otherwise afford. 5. The funds provided were used by recipients to purchase food, sanitation products, and health services. Additionally, site visits were conducted to encourage healthy eating and provide information sessions on food security and healthy sexual behaviors. 6. Despite the program's short duration, recipients increased the number of food groups consumed by 29%. The proportion of women consuming at least five out of ten predefined food groups the previous day or night rose from 34% to 60%. 7. More girls reported attending antenatal check-ups and understanding the importance of utilizing medical services, alongside improved dietary habits. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends reducing free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake for both adults and children, with a further reduction to below 5% suggested for additional health benefits. 9. WHO advises increasing potassium intake from food to control blood pressure in children aged 2–15 years. For adults, the recommended potassium intake is at least 90 mmol/day, adjusted downward for children based on their energy requirements. 10. Sodium intake should be reduced to control blood pressure in children aged 2–15 years. The maximum recommended sodium intake for adults is 2 g/day, which should also be adjusted downward for children based on their energy needs. 11. Adolescents presenting with weight loss should be assessed for underlying causes and managed accordingly. Nutritional counseling and information on achieving a healthy weight should be provided. 12. Adolescents at risk of malnutrition should be enrolled in programs offering nutritional assessment, counseling, and support. Those with active tuberculosis (TB) should receive TB diagnosis, treatment, and care per WHO guidelines. 13. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should be treated following WHO recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition. 14. Pregnant women with active TB and moderate undernutrition or inadequate weight gain should receive nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to achieve an average weekly weight gain of at least 300 g during the second and third trimesters. 15. WHO recommends fortifying staple foods like maize flour and cornmeal with iron to prevent iron deficiency, particularly in vulnerable groups such as children and women. 16. Fortification of maize flour and cornmeal with folic acid is recommended to reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs). All food-grade salt used in households and food processing should be fortified with iodine to prevent iodine deficiency disorders. 17. Red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age should be above 400 ng/mL to achieve the greatest reduction in NTDs. This threshold is useful at the population level but cannot predict individual risk. 18. Daily iron supplementation is recommended for menstruating women and adolescent girls in settings with high anemia prevalence (40% or higher) to prevent anemia and iron deficiency. 19. In malaria-endemic areas, iron supplementation for infants and children should be provided alongside public health measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. 20. Adolescents in humanitarian and fragile settings should have access to adequate nutrition, disability and injury care, violence prevention, sexual and reproductive health services, and mental health support. 21. Core health services should be accessible to adolescents with disabilities or injuries, including rehabilitation services and essential medicines in appropriate dosages and formulations. 22. Survivors of sexual and gender-based violence, including former child soldiers, should receive medical screening, clinical management, and community-based psychosocial support to aid their reintegration into families and communities. 23. Safe spaces, both virtual and physical, should be created for adolescents, including in schools, to promote peacebuilding and mental health. 24. Adolescents should be engaged in inclusive recreational activities, formal or informal education, and purposeful activities of interest. Psychological first aid techniques should be employed to support adolescents and their parents. 25. Play-based programming, including sports and play, shows promise for promoting mental health and should be considered in refugee centers and adolescent-friendly spaces.
